lead: A helical compression spring is wire coiled into a helix. Push on it and each coil twists, so the wire is a torsion bar wound into a small space. Springs store energy, absorb shock, keep parts in contact and measure force: valve springs, clutch springs, suspension coils, spring balances and railway buffers. The design links four numbers, wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D, active coils and the load, through one stress formula and one deflection formula.
prereq: You need torsion of a round bar and strain energy from the chapters on stresses.

sections.h3: Types of springs and the terms of a helical spring

blocks.text: Springs come as helical compression, helical extension and torsion springs, spiral springs (clocks), leaf springs (vehicles), disc or Belleville springs (high force in little space) and rubber springs. This chapter covers the helical compression spring.

items: Spring index C = D/d, usually 4 to 12. A small C is hard to wind and highly stressed; a large C is floppy and buckles.
Active coils Na deflect; end coils only seat the spring.
Total coils Nt: plain ends Nt = Na; plain ground Na + 1; squared, or squared and ground, Na + 2.
Solid length Ls = Nt·d (squared and ground ends) with all coils touching.
Free length Lf = Ls + δmax + gap. A common gap allowance is 15 % of δmax, so the coils never close in service.
Pitch = Lf/(Nt − 1) for squared and ground ends.

blocks.text: A load W makes each section of wire carry a torque WD/2 and a direct shear W. The torsion gives 8WD/(πd³). The curvature of the coil raises the stress on the inside of the coil, and the direct shear adds to it there. The Wahl factor K corrects for both:

blocks.where: τ is the largest shear stress, at the inside of the coil, in MPa; W in N; D and d in mm.
K is the Wahl factor (1.25 at C = 6, 1.18 at C = 8). The direct-shear factor alone is K<sub>s</sub> = 1 + 0.5/C.
δ is the axial deflection in mm; G the shear modulus (about 81 000 MPa for spring steel). The rate is k = W/δ = Gd⁴/(8D³N<sub>a</sub>) and the energy stored U = ½Wδ.

blocks.text: A spring much longer than its diameter buckles sideways like a column. If L<sub>f</sub>/D is above about 4, guide it on a rod or inside a tube.

A spring has mass as well as stiffness, so it has its own natural frequency. When one end is struck, as by a cam, a compression wave runs along the coils. If the cam's frequency, or one of its harmonics, matches the spring's natural frequency, the coils resonate: this is surge. Some coils close up while others open, the stress rises far above the static value and the valve may float off the cam.
f<sub>n</sub> is the natural frequency in Hz of a spring held between two plates; d and D in m; G in Pa; ρ the wire density in kg/m³ (7850 for steel).

Keep f<sub>n</sub> at least 15 to 20 times the operating frequency. Cures: raise f<sub>n</sub> (thicker wire, smaller D, fewer active coils), use friction dampers on the middle coils, use two concentric springs of different frequencies, or use a variable-pitch spring whose coils close one by one.

examples.question: A spring of D = 50 mm, d = 6 mm and 10 active coils carries 500 N. G = 80 000 MPa. Find the Wahl factor, largest shear stress, deflection and rate.

Design a helical compression spring (squared and ground ends) for a maximum load of 1000 N with a deflection of 25 mm at that load. Take C = 6, permissible shear 420 MPa, G = 81 370 MPa. Find d, D, N<sub>a</sub>, L<sub>s</sub>, L<sub>f</sub> and pitch, and check surge for a 10 Hz cam.
steps: L<sub>f</sub>/D = 98/42 = 2.3 < 4, so no buckling guide is needed.
examples.answer: d = 7 mm, D = 42 mm, 8 active and 10 total coils, L<sub>s</sub> = 70 mm, L<sub>f</sub> = 98 mm, pitch 10.9 mm, f<sub>n</sub> = 180 Hz.

traps: Leaving out the Wahl factor. At C = 6 it adds 25 % to the stress.
Using the outside diameter as D. D is the mean coil diameter, from wire centre to wire centre.
Using total coils in the deflection formula. Only active coils deflect.
Mixing units in the surge formula: it needs metres, pascals and kg/m³, while the stress formula is in N and mm.
Rounding N<sub>a</sub> up without rechecking δ. More coils make the spring softer, so the deflection changes.

quiz.q: Define spring index and give its usual range.
quiz.a: C = D/d, mean coil diameter over wire diameter; usually 4 to 12.

quiz.q: How many total coils does a spring with 8 active coils and squared and ground ends have?
Why is the Wahl factor greater than 1?
quiz.a: Curvature makes the shear on the inside of the coil higher than in a straight bar, and the direct shear W adds to the torsional shear there. K accounts for both.

quiz.q: A spring of rate 20 N/mm is compressed 15 mm. Find the load and the energy stored.
A valve spring has f<sub>n</sub> = 90 Hz and the cam runs at 30 Hz. Is surge likely?
quiz.a: Yes. The third harmonic of the cam motion, 3 × 30 = 90 Hz, equals f<sub>n</sub>, and f<sub>n</sub> is only 3 times the cam frequency, well below the 15 to 20 times rule.

quiz.q: At fixed W and d, D is raised from 50 to 60 mm. What happens to τ, δ and f<sub>n</sub>?
quiz.a: C rises from 8.33 to 10 and K falls from 1.176 to 1.145, but 8WD/(πd³) rises by 20 %, so τ rises from 347 to 405 MPa. δ ∝ D³ rises by 73 %. f<sub>n</sub> ∝ 1/D² falls by 31 %. The spring is softer, more highly stressed and more prone to surge.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engine valve springs are shot-peened, preset and often made with oval or beehive shapes to reduce mass and surge. Spring makers design with standards such as EN 13906 and software that includes coil clash and dynamic stress. Search for beehive valve spring and EN 13906.
